Current stream processing frameworks, such as Apache Flink and Spark Streaming, struggle to keep up with high-frequency data streams. They're inefficient in terms of hardware resource usage and, as a result, are limited to low-frequency updates (seconds or minutes). These frameworks invest significant effort in handling randomly timed events, but typically only a small percentage of that effort (around 10%) is actually used for processing high-quality data streams that occur at regular intervals. In contrast, operating systems and network protocols always synchronize periodic data streams, which means their boundaries, such as timestamps and arrivals, are perfectly known in advance. Leveraging this knowledge, we designed a specialized periodic stream processing engine called LifeStream. LifeStream's innovative architecture efficiently supports periodic data streams by desynchronizing them from CPU cycles, reducing periodic check-ins from nearly 100% to a very small percentage (<10%). With this 10x improvement, LifeStream achieves nearly 1.5x better hardware resource investment return and, in some cases, achieves 3x better performance on synthetic benchmarks and 1.5x better performance on real-world workloads (AQL) compared to top-tier general-purpose solutions.

This research paper confirms that Bertrand curves in certain geometric environments, such as BER spaces, are limited to specific curves, and demonstrates that curves in certain spaces, like KAH spaces, are not associated with their own geometric counterparts. It also reveals that a particular type of curve, the helix, does not fit the criteria for a Bertrand curve in certain geometric environments.

The application of classification models in the automotive industry, particularly in the field of traffic sign recognition, is being influenced by this research. We investigate various loss function options in neural networks, aiming to identify the most effective one. By conducting an extensive empirical study on the DVV Traffic Sign Dataset, we prioritize sign recognition accuracy. Our research involves testing different loss functions across multiple network architectures. The results show that modified loss functions, which consider sign frequency and size, yield superior accuracy compared to the standard cross-entropy loss. Notably, a proposed loss function inspired by traffic sign statistics proved most effective. This innovative loss function has been incorporated into industry-signals at a major German automotive company, optimizing traffic sign recognition performance.

This article investigates a boundary feedback control system on the 2D Navier-Stokes equations, characterized by a linear feedback controller applied to a boundary that is slanted relative to the natural coordinate system. Building upon previous findings, it is demonstrated that an exponential stabilization can be achieved with a sufficiently small feedback gain, providing a gain-margin result for this configuration. A key outcome of this research is the extension of stabilization results to cases where the angle of the slanted boundary approaches a right angle, ultimately reaching a straight boundary perpendicular to the natural coordinate system. This latter scenario was previously thought to be insufficient for guaranteeing exponential stabilization due to concerns regarding the regularity of the Stokes operator.

This research employs a comprehensive thermomechanical model to analyze the mechanical, thermal, and structural evolution of semitransparent liquid polymers caused by rapid mechanical loading. Although an ideal viscous material model was used, it effectively captured the rapid development of mechanical instabilities in liquid substances. We examined how mechanical factors induce structural changes that in turn affected the material's thermal properties and mechanical stability, leading to further structural disorder. A key mechanical parameter was identified which dictated the progression of instabilities; this parameter could represent material properties and was influenced by the development of microstructure. To identify this parameter, we proposed using experimental methods and applied this framework to simulate and predict the development of patterns seen in semitransparent liquid cyclooctadecane under rapid stretching, including various stages of instabilities, viscoelastic effects, and mechanical resonance.

To analyze the impact of spin interactions and magnetic inertia on a single--band superconductor with broken time-reversal symmetry and nematic point-group properties, we applied both mean-field theory and a Ginzburg-Landau theory near the critical transition point. In our study, we found that at the superconducting transition, strong spin-exchange and magnetic inertia can lead to the emergence of a non-zero magnetic moment in the triplet condensate, which can result in a ferromagnetic state with a finite specific heat that does not vary linearly with temperature. Furthermore, the application of a weak magnetic field can modify the energy gap and specific heat of this model. Additionally, we examined the impact of a weak magnetic field on a weak-coupling superconductor by solving the Eliashberg equations in a nematic quaternions space.

A significant challenge in developing skilled robotics agents is finding an effective way of presenting to them information that may be represented digitally.
We investigated the optimal format of external information to accelerate learning through digital means.
Initially, we tested whether good agents could be taught to less capable robotics learners by human demonstration, to expert simulation, or from real-world data.
As an alternative, we proposed a digital means of providing external information that guides the learning process of robotic agents.
We formulated this as a universal algorithm for optimizing a prior policy.
This algorithm has a range of applications, from assisting human instructors, to expert virtual trainers, or real data.
We evaluated this approach on physical robotics agents learning to navigate and manipulate objects.
The results showed that this algorithm can teach difficult navigation tasks to a physical robotics agent from digital data.
It was found to be more effective than other methods such as human demonstration, expert simulation, or self-directed learning.
This approach was also effective in teaching a physical agent to grasp a rotating 3D object from data learned by a virtual trainer.
It outperformed other methods including comparison learning, curriculum planning, or curriculum optimization.

Difference Differential Continuous Phase Modulation (DCPM) detection, although simple to implement, suffers from performance limitations due to its required two-symbol observation delay. An alternative approach, ignoring differential encoding, allows for 1-symbol delay detection but results in increased differential interference. To counter this, we propose modifying the differential detection process to achieve the same 1-symbol delay detection with reduced interference. We analyze the optimized scheme and provide its performance characteristics, including asymptotic error rate for weak signals and design guidelines. Numerical simulations demonstrate its effectiveness, showing significant improvement, up to 3 dB in SNR, compared to standard DCPM detection. We also explore its application in impulse radio communication systems, where its enhanced performance is particularly beneficial due to their inherent susceptibility to differential interference.

The number of observed black-hole neutron-star mergers is expected to surpass that of binary neutron-star mergers by an order of magnitude, yet a challenge arises from the possibility of some black-hole neutron-star merger events producing gravitational-wave signals below the threshold of multi-messenger observations. We develop a method to calculate the ratio of such "dark" events to those emitting bright electromagnetic radiation, leveraging an established approach to model the statistical distribution of observable binary neutron-star mergers. We incorporate the effects of gravitational-wave and electromagnetic emission on the detectability of our events, relying on existing research into the relationship between electromagnetic emission and the characteristics of binary neutron-star mergers. We also examine the role of core-collapse supernovae in the formation of these systems through gravitational-wave super- novovae models and find that this process significantly increases the likelihood of observable, bright events when compared to chemical evolution models. Assuming a specific type of supernovovae model, we predict that for each binary neutron-star merger merger we observe, there will be between 0.34 to 10 "dark" events, depending on the ratio of electromagnetic emission.

This study delves into the quantum capabilities and compressibility of spacetime vacuum in various thermal settings, specifically above and below the temperature of the early universe's expansion, as well as in hypothetical infinite heat scenarios. A newly devised measure, quantum capability, is employed to assess the ease with which quantum spacetime vacuum deforms, with lower values signifying increased rigidity. A crucial discovery arises from the identification of absolute maximum and minimum temperatures, along with their respective temperatures, as superconducting-like phenomena may emerge at infinite heat when thermal compaction facilitates thermal current facilitation. Notably, it is proven that thermal compaction reduces the repulsive gravitational force, ultimately enabling thermal facilitation of thermal current.

Current techniques for generating realistic rain in computer graphics and simulations are highly effective.  Less accomplished, however, is training a generator to accurately remove the rain from synthetic data.  To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel approach that decouples rain generation and removal into separate processes.  First, we introduce a rain generator module capable of producing realistic rain.  Then, we develop a discrete unrolling denoiser to remove the synthetic rain generated by our model.  To further decouple orientation and spatial information, our method employs orientation projection to create oriented rain and spatial discretization to handle spatial information.  Experiments demonstrate that our rain creation and removal models perform better than random rain models on multiple benchmark datasets.  When compared to discrete unrolling rain removal baselines, our method achieves a notable improvement of at least 16 dB in PSNR.  Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

The prominent strategies for automatically learning reward functions through group ranking are now extensively utilized in creating algorithms for games with complex rules. A widely adopted technique involves presenting users with choices between subsets of actions to efficiently navigate large state and action spaces. However, this approach has a key limitation, as each ranked cluster still represents a specific state and users must provide numerous rankings to cover the state space. To address this issue, we propose adding a second dimension to group ranking by introducing cluster descriptions that describe each ranked subset of actions. Our suggested method, called Visual Aided Cluster Ranking (VACR), leverages visual input to accelerate the learning process by allowing users to provide feedback on the data they have observed. A vital advantage of the VACR approach over traditional automated reward learning methods is its ability to efficiently navigate the trade-off users must consider between performance and effort when providing feedback, as visual data presents varying levels of information and controlability. Through comprehensive experiments conducted on Super Mario Bros, we demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over a leading alternative through statistically significant results.

A continuous range of a model's possible outcomes is often described as a continuum.
Recently, the concept of continuum has gained popularity in economics due to concerns that certain policy decisions may lead to unsustainable financial outcomes.
In this paper, the author aims to offer a unique perspective on financial and real-world continuums by utilizing a simple model that features an infinite spectrum of possible solutions.
It will be demonstrated that such continuums arise when model components possess excessive flexibility.
Furthermore, such simplicity in a basic model serves to illustrate that seemingly intricate issues, like fiscal dominance or continuum-like scenarios, ultimately boil down to a fundamental imbalance between the supply and demand for the model's core asset.
Thus, such continuums can be perceived as extreme manifestations of the same underlying phenomenon.

This study examines the invariant curvature quantity from a specific transformation and its connection to conformal geodesic flow, and we prove a maximum principle and establish an existence theorem for Q-nbn, addressing uniqueness issues by incorporating uniqueness constraints. A limit principle for Q-nbn is developed for sequence convergence, and we derive a b-nbn equation with reduced capacity charges and a related mountain pass theorem.

Research indicates that an individual's personality is a crucial factor in their propensity for making poor decisions, including those related to drug abuse.  However, personality evaluation methods are not uniform due to the existence of multiple theoretical frameworks, each proposing a different set of personality dimensions.  This research focuses on character assessment using the Five Factor Model, which is comprised of openness, conscientiousness, extroversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability.  We integrated existing personality evaluation tools to create a comprehensive set of 20 character traits that can be employed to assess an individual's risk for drug-related issues.  Analysis based on nonlinear principal component analysis revealed that all 20 character traits carry significant information, accounting for over 80% of the variance, and that these traits can be grouped into five sets of four characters each, closely linked to the Five Factor Model.  Furthermore, we demonstrated that 19 characters have an average improvement rate of 0.85 in their ability to explain individual differences, and that using this set of character traits can accurately forecast drug usage patterns, as indicated by an $R$-square value of 0.73 in a test involving 125 individuals and 25 different drugs.  This finding suggests that our approach to character evaluation may provide a beneficial supplement to existing personality assessment methods.

We introduce a significant advancement in RuleLearning for if-then reasoning, known as ATOMIC, which is an innovative approach that leverages machine common knowledge. By incorporating a pre-existing dataset of 130,000 universally applicable facts called OpenAssume, ATOMIC shows that rules learned for a specific task are more generalizable and robust to distributional changes. As a result, we see a 25% increase in accuracy on average across 10,000 simulated tasks when comparing ATOMIC to standard RuleLearning, and it also demonstrates improvements in performance on real-world datasets for generalization and robustness.

Our research introduces NISQ-HHL, a new method for efficiently solving sparse, diagonal-predominant linear systems, which are commonly found in financial applications and iterations of large AI training processes. By integrating the NISQ-HHL algorithm with a traditional optimizer like PGD or Adam, our approach leverages quantum machinery for costly matrix-vector multiplications, significantly reducing the need for hyperparameter optimization and potentially shrinking the required quantum resources by up to $O(1000)$ times, as outlined in our supplementary materials. A series of practical tests were conducted to validate the effectiveness of NISQ-HHL, including tasks such as cryptocurrency price forecasting, historical stock price pattern recognition, and the development of neural networks trained on the MNIST dataset.

Recently, pre-trained models that utilize multiple sources of information have achieved high performance across various tasks. One notable advancement is the development of a joint system that processes both speech and text, addressing several issues including data variability and the lack of sufficient speech-text pairs. Building upon these improvements, we propose a new method to train models that combine speech and text, utilizing two focused attention mechanisms: text-focused and speech-focused attention. We also introduce a simple training method called bidirectional focus to compare with other approaches. Our experiments show that the proposed models outperform both unimodal training and simultaneous training of speech and text. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of training both separate modes and then together. Our code is openly available on GitHub.

The concept of "rational points" on algebraic varieties has been extensively studied, with focus on understanding the density of these points. A key methodology employed in this field is Minowski's geometric approach, which we adapt and expand upon by introducing a rational point on a cubic surface in three-dimensional space, specifically centered around the average chord length from this point to other points on the cubic. Our objective is to utilize numerical methods to identify cubic surfaces where the average chord length remains consistent from a given rational point, and we have successfully identified two such examples, along with providing visual representations of these surfaces.

For a randomly selected uniform parking function of length $n$, the number of initial arguments equal to their corresponding values follows a non-Parking function distribution. In contrast, for the uniform symmetric random triangle function, these initial arguments are uniformly distributed among the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Additionally, the expected value of this quantity for the uniform symmetric random triangle function is approximately $0.79$ times the expected value for the uniform parking function.

investigation into the electrical characteristics of superconducting nanowires is conducted using moselectric field effect transistors, and it is observed that in certain conditions, they switch from insulating to superconducting states. This study focuses on narrow NbN nanowires with widths between 4.4 nm and 14.6 nm, and gate-induced electrostatic fields allow for maximum conductivity to be achieved in the thinnest channels. Notably, in this research, coherence of quantum phase slips is controlled by gating, and it is demonstrated that disordered superconducting systems can exhibit maximum conductivity when exposed to optimal gate control. Unexpectedly, minimum conductivity in these systems can also be governed by gating and, in some cases, exhibit characteristics similar to the critical behavior of zero-max-resistance, indicating the influence of both quantum fluctuations and Coulomb obstructions on superconducting systems.

Spectra of T-dwarfs possess significant astrophysical importance, yet their analysis remains a substantial challenge, particularly in resolving their ambiguous classification, despite discoveries of earlier M-dwarfs in the recent years.  GJ 229B, the initial recognized T-dwarf, exhibits an enigmatic type, and despite analysis of its spectrum by multiple researchers, a consensus on its type has not been reached.  In an effort to resolve this, multiple spectral models were developed using the APOLLO code to analyze near-infrared and mid-infrared data, allowing for a precise fit and determination of GJ 229B's fundamental characteristics, including the agreement or discrepancy of these findings with previous studies.  It has also been discovered that conventional chemical equilibrium calculations fail to accurately reproduce GJ 229B's unique spectrum, necessitating alternative calculations that account for kinetic effects for a deeper understanding of these type-dwarfs.

Ongoing experiments at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and the Large Hadron Collider investigate the properties of the quark-gluon medium, a state of matter believed to be formed during their collisions. To understand this medium better, physicists must analyze inelastic scattering processes involving nucleons that result in heavy ion. Our study delves into the dynamic process of high-energy nucleon interaction, considering the formation of a transient, highly compressed nuclear matter state. We explore how nucleon internal components, including nucleon quarks and gluons, as well as nucleon emitted partons, engage with this medium. Notably, we found that the inelastic scattering's outcome, such as nuclear modification factors and elliptic flow, provides valuable insights and essentially complements the information obtained from heavy ion collisions. Given its potential, we suggest that including inelastic scattering processes in theoretical models of hadronization may yield a deeper understanding of matter created in these collisions.

Predicting how a scene will change and how the camera's perspective will shift in video data is an important problem in computer vision. It's a fundamental step for tasks like scene graph generation and enables technologies like virtual cameras. However, most current models handle these aspects separately, which is a limiting factor. To tackle this, we've created an innovative framework that processes scene graph changes and camera movement channals jointly, which is a significant improvement. This framework utilizes a unique graph-to-video auto-encoder that's trained with a combination of real video data and synthetic views generated by Radiance Camera System (RCS). It's the first model of its kind to handle this joint prediction task. Our model's architecture includes a versatile decoder module that's capable of handling both prediction tasks. It's been shown that this model's performance is significantly enhanced when compared to baseline models on both forecasting tasks.

Einstein's principle of indistinguishability underlies many prominent effects  
found in gas collections of non-interacting particles, leading to significant  
consequences when interacting particles are considered.  
In this study, we investigated the impact of inter-orbital interaction between  
spin-specific states in a collectivity of Li atoms, produced a novel form of  
interaction, and sought to identify both spin-separated and mixed state outcomes  
through an intentional inter-orbital scattering process.  
By implementing this Li experiment, we discovered that the inter-orbital  
interaction induced a transition from separate state layers to a combined state  
when a minimal amount of interaction was generated, thereby demonstrating the  
significant impact of mild interactions on many-body particle systems.

The Omega baryon has long been a focus of theoretical and experimental research in hadron spectroscopy. Recently, the Particle Data Group added more data points to the existing $K_{\pi\pi}\Omega^{-}$ spectrum, highlighting an anomalous peak. In this study, we analyzed the mass and spin-parity of this peak using a quark model based on the light-front relativistic harmonic oscillator. Three distinct quark interaction models were examined, and we found that the peak could represent a $^3D_{2}$ state of the $K_{3s} \Lambda^{*}$ baryon. Additionally, we predicted more data points for single-charm $\Omega_b^-$ and double-charm $\Omega_b^+ \bar{c}c$ baryons.

Compartmental disease models typically assume individuals in a specific space interact in a randomly mixed manner, leading to infections spreading in a stochastic, well-stirred manner. Although this random interaction framework is theoretically useful, its practical application is limited due to people's tendency to engage in directed movements and remain in areas they wish to stay in, potentially creating localized outbreaks. However, urban buses provide an ideal setting to study this phenomenon due to their short trip durations and diverse passenger demographics. We conducted a randomized experiment on a real urban bus route during off-peak hours to track the spread of a marker disease, and analyzed the resulting data using a SEIR model, taking into account the bus's physical layout and travel times between stops. Our results indicate that while the random mixing framework does not accurately reflect illness spread in the bus, it still offers a beneficial baseline for creating public health interventions to prevent disease transmission during urban transit.

Every day, billions of photons with high energy pass through air and reach our eyes, causing no problems for observation or navigation. However, a significant number of these photons should theoretically birefringe and diffract slightly when compared to a single path. While this phenomenon occurs, human detectors are not sensitive enough to perceive it in quantum terms. To effectively study this, I propose using highly polarized photons to undergo diffraction in air, which can be effectively detected by glaze-covered infrared cameras or birefringent filters, even without the need to artificially increase the intensity of the light. Furthermore, this proposed method should be sensitive to any changes in the medium through which the photons travel, such as might be caused by dark matter interactions. As an educational tool, I also provide a simple computer simulation to visualize these effects.

This note presents an updated and more accessible version of the Eisenlohr-Farris method, specifically for determining completeness in partially transitive polyhedra, with full applicability to any symmetry group action on an incidence structure.

We examine the concepts and proofs related to unforgeable encryption systems.
We prove that even a minuscule amount of publicly accessible key information is
sufficient to guarantee unforgeability, which is basically equivalent to
secure decryption without the need for any secret, implying that perfect
confidentiality can be attained with only a negligible quantity of secret key
data. We further demonstrate that in the presence of an adversary capable of
learning and manipulating public keys along with interacting with an encryption
function, the notion of semantically secure ciphertext (SSC) is sufficient to
ensure unforgeability. Finally, we explore the relationship between two systems:
one featuring an adversary capable of learning and manipulating public keys and
an decryption function, and another with an adversary capable of manipulating
public keys alone. We show that in the latter scenario, the security of an
adversary capable of decrypting is ensured by the combined security of an SSC
adversary and a secure public key (SPK) adversary. We provide a new proof that
includes optimizations, an inductive approach, and a method to minimize the
required key data size. We also include proofs that incorporate improvements
over previous works.

Physical layer security is an emerging security paradigm, which is based on unique and unclonable hardware characteristics of individual devices to perform security operations such as authentication and encryption. A new security scheme, also known as physical unclonable based verification in the air (PUVA), is proposed in this study to broaden the application of physical layer security in security-sensitive operations like authentication. Although the concept of PUVA has been previously explored in paper prototypes with custom hardware, this study is the first to conduct a study on PUVA in real-world scenarios over a standard voice communication channel. A novel framework is presented in this study to evaluate the performance of PUVA in real-world settings and demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a high correct acceptance rate (99.9999999%) and low incorrect rejection rate (0.0000001%) for a device pair in typical noisy environments. Furthermore, the formulation of a key generation rate metric allows us to analyze the impact of parameters such as coding rate and observation time, providing a guideline for real-world system design. Notably, PUVA is found to be secure against a wide range of potential threats, including observation, replay attacks, and even when the adversary has partial access to the communication channel, resulting in a potential design that requires no custom hardware and minimal computational overhead.

We've analyzed the flat-band surface plasmon polaritons in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides, and discovered that certain twist angles produce doubly degenerate Rytov modes. These modes allow for extremely strong light-matter interactions due to their small charge carrier densities and large local field enhancements near the monolayer defects. For instance, the mode with the smallest size at a 54.2-degree twist angle exhibits an quality factor over one million, and the field enhancement factor is more than one thousand, creating ideal conditions for generating single photons and ultra-fast switching with low loss. Notably, this system provides access to controllable Kerr nonlinearity and can achieve single-mode operation at pump powers less than a milliwatt.

This research paper expands the properties of a gradient Ricci soliton defined on a Sasakian manifold. We provide a mathematical expression for the scalar curvature of a gradient Ricci soliton on such a manifold, establish a relationship between the Ricci curvature and the gradient of a potential function on a hypersurface of the manifold, and establish an upper bound for the entropy of a family of diffusion processes. Additionally, we demonstrate that if a gradient Ricci soliton is defined on a Sasakian manifold that is also an $\eta$-Ricci soliton or a conformal gradient Ricci soliton, it must be semi-Einstein. This research generalizes and expands upon previous results found in existing literature.

This study offers a comprehensive analysis of how stellar winds and solar systems operate, then contrasts this knowledge with that of celestial bodies and their solar environments. Research indicates that the presence of a magnetic field, solid surface, and atmosphere in a planet or moon all influence its solar system. We examine the effects of a planet's or moon's surface on its magnetosphere when exposed to solar winds and discuss how these interactions vary due to additional factors such as an internal magnetic field. Additionally, the effects of atmospheric interactions on plasma dissipation within a planet's ionosphere are explored. A key distinction between celestial bodies and planets lies in their atmospheres; while stars have massive atmospheres that significantly impact plasma dissipation, stars have thin outer layers that result in minimal ionization.

Spin-orbit proximity effects result in enhanced spin-orbit coupling in a material in contact with a high-spin-orbit-coupling metal, which has significant implications for thin-film applications. This study focuses on understanding the mechanisms at play in modern magnetic random access memory structures consisting of cobalt oxide coated with bismuth. First-principles calculations reveal that electron hybridization between the bi and co layers is minimal, leading to dominant spin-orbit coupling from bi and considerable electron conductance from co. Notably, the data also show that electron scattering at the interface influences the Hall conductivity in the co layer, with observations made regarding how magnetic disorder and orientation affect scattering at the bi/co interface.

This paper utilizes the Jumarie type fractional derivative to solve the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation associated with a generalized Mie-like potential in multiple dimensions. By applying the semi-it mapping technique, a closed-form solution to the problem is obtained and verified through a direct substitution method. Numerical illustrations and graphical representations are obtained and analyzed for a specific set of parameters and fractional parameters. This approach provides a novel and effective means of addressing complex physical problems involving fractional calculus.

We have developed a novel approach to improve the reliability of neural networks through the concept of Lipschitz consistency. This approach is grounded in the principle that effective prediction networks should adhere to a fairness standard, ensuring that no single feature is given undue significance. We formulate this as an optimization problem, incorporating a consistency term in the objective function to ensure that the network does not overvalue any single feature. We prove a convergence result for a specific algorithm proposed by Mhaskar and Poon (2019), and demonstrate through numerical experiments that this method yields robust predictions, reducing the likelihood of overfitting and enhancing performance on novel, unrelated data.

Long Short-Term Memory networks have gained significant attention in numerous speech patterns research studies due to their effectiveness in addressing sequence issues. To evaluate the capabilities of an LSTM model, we utilised the Basque Agreement Corpus (BAC), a resource designed for assessing speech patterns more rigorously and RST-basque, an existing Basque probabilistic context-free grammar rule set. Our evaluation of an LSTM model that utilises the BAC as training data showed a high accuracy of 97.88%, but our analysis of the Basque verbal auxiliary selected by the model revealed notable difficulties with certain agreement categories, notably when dealing with the 3rd singular person, singular/dual/plural forms, and gender. Our findings suggest that while the BAC is an excellent resource for training machine learning models to capture Basque agreement, certain aspects of the language pose significant challenges for an LSTM model to grasp.

We used a global network of telescopes, including 11 on the Very Large Array, to observe the HD 80606 b planet's behavior as it passes before its host star. This allowed us to create a highly precise trajectory for the planet. By analyzing 11 transit events, we were able to build an incredibly accurate schedule for upcoming transits, which will be useful for future transits that the James Webb Space Telescope and other near-infrared telescopes can detect. These observations will help us study the composition of the planet's atmosphere. However, our data suggests that the previously known eccentricity of the planet is inaccurate, likely caused by inaccuracies in the astrometry of the stars, which leads to a significantly different value for the planet's distance from its host star during transits. As a result, our data suggests a significantly different composition for the planet, either a rocky world with a thick atmosphere or one made mostly of gas, with very different predictions for future transits being tested by both teams of researchers.

Virtual reality gaming offers an engaging and adaptable setting for hands-on assessment and customization of exercises to improve or retrain specific skills. By employing statistical models of player behavior, we can create a personalized baseline and measure progress as a game is adjusted, offering a structured approach to evaluating the development of particular abilities. This study explores the potential of utilizing statistical models in a motion rehabilitation context to analyze walk-through gameplay on the VR reWalk Trainer, a program designed to evaluate and retrain balance and walking balance through a virtual road. Balance retraining is modeled after driving, while walking balance is similar to the experience of operating a vehicle. A study was conducted with nine participants who provided balance and walking balance data as they navigated the virtual road. The participants' performance was compared to a statistical aggregate representing normal driver behavior, and they demonstrated balance and walking balance proficiency comparable to experienced drivers. Notably, two participants who had previous balance disorders showed significant improvements following the training. We suggest that balance and walking balance can be effectively measured and retrained by utilizing models of normal driver behavior, offering a promising approach to leveraging virtual reality for balance rehabilitation.

This work offers a novel method for approximating certain functionals on broken mappings through a series of progressively more flexible piecewise smooth approximations. The approach is designed to accommodate configurations involving multiple discontinuities and is shown to converge under specific conditions, as described by a variational formula. The phase-field method finds practical applications in modeling materials that undergo complex deformation and is related to an analogous scheme used for simulating fracture propagation.

We examine a new type of leptoquark called an electroweak vector, denoted as $G^{*}$, which has three generations and is odd in charge-parity. This type of leptoquark is related to the Drell-Yan process, specifically $pp\to G^{*}\bar{G}^{*}\to t\bar{t}$ production. To study this more accurately, we developed calculations at next-to-leading order in QCD with consistent parton showers. The analysis of rapidity and $p_{T}$ distributions of the top quark shows that including effects of parton showers improves the agreement with current experimental data from the LHC. Additionally, by analysing $pp \to t_{\rm jet} + X$ data at the LHC, we were able to derive constraints on the mass of the $G^{*}$ leptoquark, yielding a lower limit of 2.44 TeV when considering a specific value for the $G^{*}$-top-photon coupling. These findings will be incorporated into the upcoming TTHTopTere data from the LHC.

Nuclear medicine imaging is reduced-dose or no-dose based on external beam imaging for diagnostic purposes due to lower quality images obtained from low-resolution low-dose PET. This research is focused on reducing the dose of PET using a single-modality approach that is reduced-dose or no-dose based on external beam imaging with a single network. A preliminary reduced-dose approach is introduced to reduce the dose of PET using external beam imaging (CT) for diagnostic purposes. For a more challenging scenario of no-dose PET, implicit generation is proposed using an external beam imaging (CT) guided approach. To tackle distribution shifts caused by noise and imaging artifacts, reduced-dose external beam imaging (CT) data is simulated. Implicit generation is proposed in response to the appearance of real data. Residual learning is modified to reduce the influence of noise. A reduced-dose PET dataset is created to evaluate performance. Evaluation metrics include mean squared error, structural similarity and PET-reality perception. Results indicate reduced-dose PET outperforms PET-only and PET with external beam imaging (CT) reference methods. Reduced-dose PET also surpasses PET-Real in terms of scores. Reduced-dose PET is also evaluated in a no-dose PET scenario. Reduced-dose PET performs competitively with PET-reality perception metrics in no-dose PET scenario. Model robustness is enhanced against data distribution shifts caused by noise and external beam imaging (CT) artifacts. Improved performance and PET-plausibility are achieved through

This study focuses on personalization techniques used in recommending items,
harnessing users' data to tailor suggestion lists to their preferences. We examine
how to balance personalized learning with protecting user data, utilizing the
framework of continual classification under data constraints. We modelize a
scenario where a recommendation system learns from user interactions with user
profiles, remaining stable when user preferences change and adapting when they
do. We develop a new classification problem variant and a corresponding algorithm
capable of adapting to user preference shifts. We propose two algorithms for solving
both problems, and through user studies, we validate our approach to customized,
privacy-preserving recommendation learning.

This paper undertakes a theoretical analysis of current neural coreference resolution methods to identify their common characteristics and challenges.
Our research reveals a prevailing tendency towards reliance on local features and surface-based reasoning in coreference resolution, which contradicts the fundamental principles of linguistics and results in issues like the "popularity bias" problem.
Drawing from Centering Theory and the concept of a focus of attention, our work introduces a novel attention-focused framework and demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating direction-sensitive features, ultimately paving the way for significant improvements in coreference resolution performance.

This paper provides an overview of the most current research on several graph drawing problems, including induced planarity, double planarity, and three various edge-disjoint planar subgraphs. We then focus specifically on upward planarity and review related parameters, such as maximum degree, bag-width, pathwidth, and spine width. Upward planarity is a crucial property for visualizing algorithms and data flow in directed graphs. We then discuss parameterized approaches for determining graphs that possess upward planarity, particularly those with small maximum degree, width parameters, and spine width.

We have developed a novel approach to automate the configuration of computer systems using a language inspired by Make, uniquely suited to managing dependent software. This approach not only streamines the process of getting multiple systems up and running but also facilitates the replication of ground truth data for machine learning projects, a task often underestimated in complexity. As a case study, we've applied this approach to establish a unified infrastructure for machine learning on several machines, and to set up machine-to-machine communication in PFIT2019, and to establish a machine with a similar learning infrastructure to that of a machine learning lab at a machine learning company, and to fully automate the setup of a machine for a ground truth dataset used in a machine learning paper, and to fully automate the setup of a machine for a ground truth dataset used in a machine learning paper, and to fully automate the setup of a machine with a fully functional implementation of a machine learning algorithm, and to fully automate the setup of a machine with a fully functional implementation of a machine learning algorithm, and to fully automate the setup of a machine with a fully functional implementation of a machine learning algorithm, and to fully automate the setup of a machine with a fully functional implementation of a machine learning algorithm, and to fully automate the setup of a machine with a fully functional implementation of a machine learning algorithm.

The conventional entanglement measure, known as the reduced density matrix method, follows a different procedure for calculating the entanglement of an operator pair compared to the operator-squared method introduced by Haah and Shen. To investigate this discrepancy, we expand the operator pair in a basis of local fields and demonstrate that the two approaches yield comparable outcomes when the expansion is limited to a few terms, or when the operator supports naturally overlap with each other. Furthermore, the expansion method reveals a power-law increase in entanglement as the operator separation grows, consistent with prior numerical findings. Ultimately, we conclude that the operator-squared method effectively captures the entanglement properties of complex operators if their spatial distribution is considered.

Recently, utilizing signal strength to determine distance through wireless networks, specifically Range Estimation (RE), has gained significant interest. RE's accuracy can be significantly enhanced through the employment of reference data by methods such as Circular Rejection (CR). However, there exists a limitation to this approach, as it tends to overestimate ranges for signals that follow non-circular patterns. To overcome this issue, the proposal put forth in this paper involves training a supervised machine learning classifier in WiFi frames to accurately predict range values. Initially, we examine various features within WiFi frames and subsequently, a machine learning model is trained to forecast range values based on these features. Our experimental results indicate that our proposed method can achieve high accuracy in RE, surpassing traditional techniques like CR and Maximum Likelihood (ML).

We employ numerical simulations to examine the stability of a spherical structure, composed of self-gravitating stars rotating around a central black hole, and discover that such a dyson shell collapses due to radial oscillations amplified by two-body interactions and the gravitational capture of stars by the black hole. However, adding a minimal angular momentum to maintain stars in distant orbits preserves the integrity of the dyson shell.

In today's complex and interconnected world, IT services are integral to our daily operations, but with this integration come potential security risks and reliability issues. To address these concerns, we propose an innovative approach to ensure that IT services meet agreed-upon quality standards and remain secure, by utilizing peer-to-peer technology for detecting service level agreement breaches in a decentralized, autonomous manner. This method involves embedding a small detection component within each peer's system, which is responsible for monitoring and analyzing data from multiple sources to identify anomalies, security breaches, and other deviations from the service level agreement. This detection component leverages its stored historical information to make decisions, reducing the burden on IT systems and enhancing overall reliability. By incorporating cryptographic techniques for secure, private communication, we offer a promising pathway for organizations to identify IT service level agreement breaches in a decentralized, blockchain-based environment, ultimately leading to more robust and trustworthy IT service management.

We investigate how changing the electron beam configuration affects its stability against disruptions caused by RF field feedback in an energy recovery linac. Specifically, we examine an aluminum-cavity ERL at 1.8GHz and find that the relationship between the beam's longitudinal profile and its stability is not consistent. However, we identify a way to restore this relationship by implementing a filtering function based on a Hermite polynomial. This optimal filling configuration enhances the beam's stability by a factor of 2 compared to standard configurations and has significant implications for designing high-current beams in future ERLs and linear colliders.

Properly understanding how neutrons scatter is crucial for accurately measuring neutrons using all modern detection techniques. Currently, there is no reliable method to fully grasp neutron scattering across all energy levels due to difficulties with detecting low-energy neutrons on the order of eV. This method presents an innovative, compact detection system consisting of six scintillator blocks, each containing six layers of high-density CH material and silicon photomultiplier readouts. By combining neutron scattering data from six different angles and four energy layers, this system can calculate the total neutron cross-section from neV to MeV. This all-digital detection system offers a comprehensive way to measure neutron flux in a single experiment, potentially paving the way for a more complete narrative in future experiments, such as those involving sterile neutrinos.

Laboratory experiments investigated submicroscopic dust particle interactions in rising temperatures to understand how the composition of particles, specifically carbonaceous chondrites and olivine, affects their sticking characteristics as they heat up. It was discovered that in colder temperatures (below approximately 400 K), particles maintain the same sticking properties as previously observed, with no significant difference between carbonaceous chondrites and olivine. However, in higher temperatures (above approximately 400 K), carbonaceous chondrites showed a decline in stiffness and an increase in damping, indicating structural degradation, whereas olivine showed a decrease in damping and increased stiffness, indicating structural strengthening. These findings suggest that organic material present in carbonaceous chondrites loses its integrity when exposed to rising temperatures, in contrast to silicate minerals which actually become more robust. This difference in behavior has implications for planetary formation, specifically influencing dust growth rates, internal planet structure, and the distribution of organic matter throughout the solar system.

Supervised dimensionality reduction techniques facilitate efficient data visualization and straightforward data analysis by generating compact student projections that retain critical information. In recent years, numerous linear and non-linear dimensionality reduction methods have been developed with enhanced performance, leading to diverse evaluation metrics that assess their effectiveness. These evaluations consider both classification and clustering aspects to comprehensively gauge a technique's ability to group similar data points and distinguish between different classes. To provide an R platform for both local fisher discriminant analysis and a associated extension, local fisher discriminant analysis +, we have created the lfda package, enabling users to apply these methods to their data and visualize the results.

Multi-robot exploration often involves navigating complex environments with obstacles and unknown terrain. To overcome this challenge, copy learning techniques enable a follower robot to emulate a leader robot, avoiding obstacles and maintaining a fixed distance for effective information transmission. However, existing methods struggle to handle nonlinear constraints and evasive maneuvers due to the loss of optimality when using optimal control techniques. To address this limitation, a novel copy learning control method is proposed for a follower robot tracking an unknown trajectory of an evasive leader robot while maintaining a fixed linear distance and avoiding obstacles in real-time. This method involves estimating the unknown linear velocity of the leader and compensating for the nonlinear connection and tracking errors to achieve optimal performance. A stability analysis proves the closed-loop system's convergence, and simulation results demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness in various scenarios.

We have calculated the one-loop central-emission vertex for two colorless bosons, which can be emitted at any point along an $N$-point amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. This calculation validates a previously made conjecture by Carrazeda, Frederico, and Thomas. To achieve this, we utilized on-shell methods and made the process more straightforward by first establishing an on-shell recursion relation for a specific amplitude, which involves multiple gluons emitted with a particular symmetry, ultimately allowing us to derive the one-loop central-emission vertex.

Within this study, we examined a novel topological superfluid (TSS) that emerges in the spin-singlet Rashba Hubbard model with non-zero and unequal chemical potentials for the two spin components. Using a non-perturbative strong-coupling expansion, we investigated how the superfluid order arises in this model and determined that the TSS phase coexists with non-trivial Z2 spin textures in Rashba rotors doped with near-half an integer number of atoms per site. These results indicate that TSS can be achieved in the spin-singlet Rashba Hubbard model without the need for spin-orbit coupling symmetry.

Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigated a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate and found an previously unreported superconducting impurity state. This state appears as point defects that give rise to a quantum interference pattern. By analyzing this pattern at various temperatures and dopings, it was found that the structure of the defect changes from a square lattice to a rotated square lattice for underdoped samples, and occurs at the $d$-wave nodal direction for overdoped samples. The rotation of the grid likely indicates a vortex state, and the fact that the state appears within the superconductor implies that it is a 'square' super-Vorbeuf-Legrand (VL) domain. If this is indeed the case, it provides evidence that high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates may be on the verge of a quantum phase transition to a different flux state.

We investigate the macroscopic behavior of molten polymer brushes on stretched substrates, 
discovered to form distinct microscale molten droplets or "end droplets" near the substrate 
tips that contribute to a negligible overall volume. To improve upon previous theories 
capable of handling only tapered and bent geometries, we develop a comprehensive framework 
that accounts for stretched, molten polymer brushes of any complex substrate configuration. This 
framework provides a direct method to calculate the total end exclusion area based on the 
polymers' inherent tendency to avoid stretching and bending deformations, offering a clear 
measure of end exclusion area in terms of the stretched substrate profile. As a result, this 
end exclusion area can be used to calculate the free energy of the system and predict 
observable overall extensions. This new theory also yields a straightforward equation for 
average extension, which can be easily solved numerically. Notably, this end exclusion effect 
is found to significantly impact average extensions, accounting for at least a half of the observed 
extension in stretched polymer brushes. This effect is particularly pronounced in coils and loops 
that contribute little to the observed overall extension in polymer brushes. This end 
exclusion area concept can be easily calculated for any polymer loop in any configuration 
of stretched, molten polymer brushes. This end exclusion effect is found to be highly relevant 
to observed contact area in adhesives and also has a direct impact on the average extension
