Given a graph G and a subset S of its vertices, a graph-theory concept known as a "metric generator" or "resolving set" allows us to uniquely locate any vertex in G by examining its distances to the points in S. We investigate the role of simplified subgraphs, formed by removing edges of length greater than one, in relation to this idea. Our analysis reveals that for most graphs, these simplified subgraphs still serve an equivalent purpose to the original subgraphs. We derive a corresponding parameter called the "shortened metric dimension" and demonstrate several of its properties. Moreover, we establish specific conditions and examples for graphs where the traditional and simplified dimensions differ, and we derive the former for some particular graphs and obtain upper bounds for others.

We've utilized machine learning techniques to enhance whole-sky maps and identify variable sources beyond traditional methods. Recent advancements in machine learning have made it possible to analyze astronomical data and produce whole-universe charts that highlight variable sources with greater precision. We examined two techniques: a traditional method and one based on machine learning, evaluating their effectiveness in identifying variable sources. The machine learning approach, specifically a gradient boosting method, processed nearly a decade of high-energy observations from a satellite, and was found to produce more accurate whole-universe charts and identified more variable sources than the traditional method. We also explored the stability of variable sources and tested different statistical models and source selection thresholds. The results from the machine learning method also led to more coherent structures in certain astronomical objects. We believe these techniques have nearly astronomical source level precision and may result in significant breakthrough discoveries, with further improvements expected as machine learning advances continue.

A random dictatorship mechanism is an $n$-ary generalization of a serial dictator, and we demonstrate that for any distribution of random dictatorships, there exists an associated transformation that produces a canonical form. This form either exhibits roughly $\sqrt{n}$ times more efficiency than serial dictatorships (when dealing with public goods), or it exhibits roughly $\sqrt{n}$ times more equity. These outcomes imply that random dictatorships can deliver either $\sqrt{n}$ times more efficiency or $\sqrt{n}$ times more equity compared to serial dictatorships, and we provide an illustrative protocol for achieving this in the case of public goods.

We developed an algorithm to identify binary asteroids in past Pan-STARRS1 images, 
concluding that approximately 0.8% to 2.8% of 1157 examined asteroids are binary systems. 
This estimate ranges from 0.8% (conservative case) to 2.8% (liberal case), 
with 2.8% being the most probable scenario. 
To detect binary asteroids, we utilized the Pan-STARRS1's 700-kilopixel, 
7-meter PSF-corrected, -1.9 magnitude images captured between 2009 and 2012, 
analyzing 1.1 terabytes of data from 1.15 million asteroids during the period. 
Our detection method involved representing each asteroid as a difference of two sources 
within an extended source model and employing a maximum likelihood approach 
to estimate the model's parameters, with a primary focus on the distance between 
the binary components. 
We established an 11-dimensional likelihood ratio as our detection criterion 
and identified 13 mass-ratio binaries with a separation of at least 2 pixel 
and a likelihood ratio greater than 5 standard deviations out of 1157 asteroids 
selected with a magnitude range of 11 to 14 and a rate of 1 per cubic magnitude. 
Given the observational limitations, 
our findings suggest the mass ratio for these binaries may

This research employs network data to develop and assess a hybrid linear model.
We utilize generalized least squares and ordinary least squares to analyze the model's responses to various exogenous variables, considering both degree and ego networks.
Using the Sarson-Pereira-Rodriguez (SPR) dataset, we examine a model of social influence where individuals' behaviors are impacted by the behaviors of their friends and those of their friends' friends.
Notably, we address a common oversight in previous studies by using the SPR dataset to test and analyze a linear model of social influence.
Our results indicate that the data support the hypothesis that self-centeredness, derived from one's own network, deters criminal activity, whereas being aware of the patterns in the network between others promotes good civic behavior.
Moreover, we are among the first to apply a straightforward, interpretable approach to criminal behavior prediction that outperforms a leading machine learning method when using the SPR dataset.

This study introduces novel expressions for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral and differential operators of a composite function, building on previous work by Kaczor (2014) and Samko (1987, 1993, 1999, 2007). Additional properties of these operators, including the Cauchy formula and an operator identity, are also derived for functions of multiple variables. Furthermore, a new approach to the Variable-Order Grunwald-Letnikov differential operator is developed.

The concept of spatial audio has evolved over the past few decades and will play an even more critical role in upcoming metaverse applications, particularly in driving spatial audio processing and signal processing technologies. This paper addresses the challenge of recovering a two-dimensional signal from one-dimensional measurements, using the method of spatial spectrogram recovery that accounts for frequency-dependent variations. Specifically, this work provides an in-depth analysis of the regression-based approach using limited measurements and random probed frequencies. The study focuses on least-squares methods, especially the recursive least-squares algorithm. For key assumptions related to parabolic scaling and condition number, this research offers precise, quantifiable limits in O-notation. The findings presented here are novel contributions to the field.

We introduce the second generation of visualizing and analyzing spectral data tools, known as RCSEDev2, designed to facilitate the graphical examination of object imaging and associated spectra on a web platform. Researchers can easily access this application via any web browser, allowing them to load and evaluate 2D spectral cubes or catalogs of objects' spectra from standard formats like FITS, FIBS-K, and JSON. The RCSEDev2 application is particularly useful for participants of community-driven projects, allowing them to swiftly assess spectral cubes or spectra of objects before including them in the project's dataset. The tools were originally created for the COMICS and RadioSTRANGERS projects but have the potential to serve a broader community engaged in optical astronomy and stratigraphy research.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean's inception is linked to the Natal Fissure in South Africa, a 20 to 25 million-year-old rift system characterized by diverse features, including normal and oblique normal faults, strike-slip faults, and significant fault lengths exceeding 500 kilometers. This study gathers and compiles the stratigraphic ages and fault movement data from existing field reports, integrating them with new field observations. Our analysis indicates multiple phases of extension along the Natal fissure system during different time periods. In a努ral segment, the main phase of extension occurred between 20 and 55 million years ago, whereas the southern phase experienced the main phase between 55 million years ago and present day. In East Africa, the main phase of extension between 25 and 55 million years ago led to the formation of the South Marginal Fault. These findings suggest two distinct mechanisms responsible for the formation of the South Atlantic and East African rifts, potentially occurring simultaneously in some areas, in contradiction to the conventional hypothesis of a synchronized 2-phase extensional process across the margin.

When working with medical image segmentation, a significant challenge arises due to the lack of available data and noisy labels that hinder label propagation and section refinement.  To address these issues, some techniques employ unsupervised learning to expand section accuracy and use convex optimization to refine kidney segmentation accuracy.  Yet, these approaches frequently encounter difficulties with noisy labels and result in limited performance improvements.  Taking advantage of the self-supervised learning capacity, some researchers have begun to explore methods to enhance medical image segmentation.  To tackle section loss from inaccurate labels, we developed an innovative self-supervised information optimization strategy.  To address boundary section loss from missing sections, we designed a boundary-sensitive mechanism.  Integrating this technique into convex optimization frameworks, our method efficiently addresses section issues and refines medical image segmentation.  Despite utilizing only fully annotated data and requiring no additional unsupervised or convex optimization modules, our method k demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques on multiple datasets including P-KID, RSNA, and MMWHS.

We introduce the Games AI Dungeon Master (GADM) challenge, a new task for game AI that involves leading a fantasy adventure with a diverse group of characters in Dungeons and Dragons. Successfully leading this adventure requires the AI to collaborate with human players, make strategic decisions, manage character development, and create a balanced and engaging experience. We establish a framework for specifying in-game character intentions using a formal theory-based approach, which enables assessment of the AI's ability to comprehend and respond to human thoughts. Furthermore, we present a method for learning these intentions through interactions with human players using Symbolic Reinforcement Learning. Through experiments, we demonstrate that the AI can effectively lead memorable and satisfying adventures by combining this learning capability with careful management of character progression and game dynamics. Our framework provides a foundation for future research into leading fantasy adventures with AI character.

This paper proposes a framework for identifying lexical semantic shifts, also known as word sense changes, which have been neglected in previous research. Initially, our framework employs LexicalCorpus to pinpoint potential candidates for semantic shift analysis. To evaluate these candidates, we developed a framework that combines distributional analysis and human judgment. This framework first calculates the stability of a word's representation by measuring the consistency of its vector across different time periods. Then, humans assess whether the meanings of words have shifted by comparing their representations from different periods. Ultimately, our framework ranks the candidates to identify the most significant lexical semantic shifts.

We propose a new set of functions related to the transverse momentum of outgoing hadrons, which we refer to as functions of $k_\perp$, and provide a definition for a (quasi)parton distribution function that depends on $k_\perp$, denoted as $\langle x, \vec{K}_\perp| \hat{\rho} |x', -\vec{K}_\perp\rangle$ (or its equivalent in a lattice context). The relationship between these functions and traditional Boer-Mulders functions is established, and we offer computational methods for calculating these functions using both perturbative and Lattice QCD approaches. The necessary formalism to describe these functions in a Lorentz-invariant manner, or within the framework of the SCET effective theory, or the twist-3 SCET, is also briefly outlined.

The three-dimensional structure and stability of knotted proteins are maintained through their coiled backtracks into knottopologies. Despite this understanding, there is still debate about how these proteins form their knottopologies in the living organisms. It is believed that solvent conditions and thermal fluctuations contribute to the entanglement of the protein backbones into knottopologies. Due to their sensitivity to topological changes, it is essential to analyze protein backbones in their native states by fitting them to idealized models, recognizing that other factors like side-chain lengths and bond angles are neglected. By applying topological methods to the protein backbones, researchers can gain valuable insights into their knotting properties from their native states. In this study, we focus on three knotted proteins (Phage P23-5J3, Treprostinin A, and Knt1) and explore possible bending pathways that would transform their knottypes. We identify bending pathways that would minimally increase the knotting properties and eliminate bending pathways that would significantly decrease the knotting properties. These results indicate that in their native states, the proteins are stabilized by specific bending pathways that prevent them from untangling into different knottypes. Understanding the factors that maintain these bending pathways, such as amino-acid interactions, could provide insights into the folding process of these proteins.

To address the mystery of dark energy, a solution known as early dark energy has emerged as the most prominent candidate. The influence of early dark energy is noted in the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure generated after the universe's expansion. By incorporating Planck and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) data, researchers gained deeper insights into the properties of early dark energy. Using a method called the profile likelihood, a 95% confidence level constraint on the early dark energy fraction was obtained. Notably, this approach avoided reliance on the $\Lambda$CDM model and, by bypassing the effects of early and late dark energy on the cosmic microwave background acoustic horizon, provided a more accurate description of early dark energy. The study also explored the relationship between early dark energy and the Hubble tension, a discrepancy between local and universe-scale measurements of the Hubble constant.

We've established that the symplectic mapping class group of the blowup of the $2n$-torus, denoted as $\mathrm{Symp}_{0}(\mathbb{T}^{2n},\blowup 1,\delta)$, is connected for sufficiently small values of $\delta$, specifically when it's less than some $\delta_{0}$ that varies depending on $n$. This finding is notable because it contradicts a previously believed general rule which posited that the mentioned group would be infinite for all values of $\delta$ less than $1/9$. We reached this conclusion by employing an inductive argument on the number $\kappa$ which denotes the number of blown-up points, establishing several key properties of the symplectic Hurwitz graph. These insights allowed us to prove that any two symplectic diffeomorphisms could be linked via a path of length at most $4\kappa$ in the graph, involving transitions in regions of the Hurwitz space that have a boundary.

A rigorous mathematical analysis has been undertaken to enhance the understanding of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which is associated with spontaneous symmetry breaking in quantum field theories. Various expressions for the ground state energy's behavior, resulting from imposed symmetries and their subsequent violations, are presented using macroscopic scales and their impacts on the theorem's aspects, such as the soft mode. Additionally, the limitations and potential improvements of the $\epsilon$-representation are illustrated through precise, albeit extended, computational examples.

Current methods for creating artificial counterfactual world knowledge that generate human-like reasoning have significant limitations due to their reliance on constrained generation, resulting in the loss of numerous plausible alternatives. We introduce a novel, automated technique for extracting phrasal counterfactuals (FCE) from a pre-trained language model, a method that surpasses traditional baselines in maintaining semantic diversity while preserving syntactic accuracy. Our experimentation shows that the FCE method captures a high proportion of valid semantic sentences that convey the same meaning as human-generated counterparts when used in a language model's understanding assessment. We further demonstrate the robustness of neural-extracted counterfactuals in preventing overfitting to specific linguistic patterns during the domain adaptation process. Our study suggests that incorporating the FCE method into optimization frameworks can significantly enhance reasoning capabilities alongside other beneficial effects.

The Total Coloring Conjecture was first proposed in 1987 by offman and later various researchers worked on proving it for different types of graphs. In 2013, Zhu suggested a more restrictive version of this theory called sum distinguishing total coloring and defined the corresponding chromatic number. The current paper aims to find sum distinguishing total colorings for a range of circulant graphs and identifies their chromatic numbers according to this concept.

Researchers utilized magnetospectroscopy to investigate the origins of magnetic ordering in cubic Heusler films of InMnSn, which were grown on graphene/Al$_2$O$_3$ using remote, van der Waals or pinhole epitaxy. By comparing magnetic properties and epitaxial balances, a method was developed to identify each type of growth. Notably, magnetic moments in pinhole epitaxy were found to be enhanced relative to bulk, indicating increased magnetic coupling. Furthermore, epitaxial balance was shown to influence magnetic ordering, which could be leveraged in adjusting the magnetic behavior of $\text{In}_2$MnSn, which displayed reduced magnetic moments and Curie temperatures. These findings highlight the significance of epitaxial balance in governing the magnetic properties of $\text{In}_2$MnSn and suggest that adjusting this factor along with composition and structural integrity offers novel avenues for epitaxial compensation.

This paper explores a new code type called $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which have gained interest due to their ability to efficiently represent codes of prime power length using the chain ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ and their connection to $\mathbb{Z}_p^3$-linear codes. This work establishes MacWilliams identities and a distance formula for these codes, while also providing a theorem on the rank of their generator matrices over various $\mathbb{Z}_{p^i}$ modules. Our research reveals that the null space of such a code is equivalent to the union of null spaces of its $\mathbb{Z}_p$ subcodes, which further implies that the dimension of the code is equal to the sum of the dimensions of its constituent $\mathbb{Z}_p$ subcodes.

The dynamics of polymer plugs moving through tubes due to the injection of one end, with no resistance at the other, are theoretically analyzed and verified through experiments and simulations. In a new set of experiments, we observe the position of an ideal polymer mass along a horizontal tube during its motion, caused by steady force applied at one end. The distribution of polymer mass is now typically represented as a profile, and we have collected an extensive set of ideal polymer plug data to expand the info available, giving ideal polymer plug profiles a comprehensive form.

The current single positive label dataset annotation method leads to a significant waste of labeling resources and a misallocation of labeling efforts, ultimately leading to a failure in obtaining dataset samples that carry multiple labels. To address this issue, a method is proposed for extracting dataset samples that carry multiple labels, utilizing a pre-trained model to apply binary classification labels already obtained, in a manner similar to prioritizing multi-label samples. Furthermore, a novel strategy is proposed to efficiently allocate dataset labeling efforts by prioritizing multi-label samples. To validate the proposed approach, the method is applied to a specific dataset, resulting in a notable increase of multi-label samples. Consequently, the proposed method is shown to be both theoretically justified and highly effective in practice.

This research provides an upper bound for energy growth over time in the time-fractional Caglar phase-field model and its variant with an modified cosine term. The study verifies that the energy increase rate is proportional to $t^{1-\alpha}$, where the constant of proportionality is positive for values of $\alpha$ between 0 and 1. The results are consistent with previously discovered time-dependent lower and upper bounds for various time-fractional PDEs and their corresponding integer-order counterparts. The study also introduces new methods and techniques to establish the energy growth condition for the time-fractional Caglar phase-field model. The findings are reinforced numerically.

The prevailing interpretation of quantum theory is often referred to as the "measurement problem," yet this paper argues that confusion arises not from the act of measurement itself but from an inadequate mathematical framework for representing observations and states. We introduce a categorical adjunction that clearly separates observations from states in the study of physical systems. This approach demonstrates that the standard measurement process is not inherently part of quantum mechanics but rather an external influence. Moreover, we propose that measurements could be modeled using monoidal categories and that the resulting dynamics can be understood through a process of unraveling these observations. This approach provides evidence that a proposed rigidity theorem supports this unifying perspective.

We propose a new theory to explain why some nearby energy-bursting galaxies emit high-energy gamma-rays, specifically those with magnetic fields that emanate from disk-shaped structures trapped in the galaxies' central engines. These structures, which are subject to intense magnetic fields, may be responsible for gamma-rays produced deep within the galaxies' engines by a process called pion decay. The theory predicts that the gamma-rays will be suppressed by photons interacting with electrons to create pairs of gamma-ray photons, but this process is inhibited because the magnetic fields redirect the gamma-rays and the electrons in opposite directions, trapping them in the disk-shaped structures. We estimate that gamma-rays could be maintained above detection thresholds for thousands of years, which is consistent with gamma-ray emissions from the galaxies NGC 1088, NGC 4945, and NGC 5548 that have been observed by the Fermi satellite.

This research reexamines well-known mean-variance optimization by shifting focus from individual asset allocation to entire portfolio allocation, moving away from traditional rebalancing methods. Instead, it introduces a novel technique known as partial portfolio replication, which involves creating new positions outside an existing portfolio to achieve target returns without altering the original asset selection. Analyzing this method's risk and return characteristics, the study demonstrates its alignment with mean-variance optimization characteristics and provides an scalable solution for portfolio optimization at large. The portfolio replication approach also avoids transaction costs and exhibits a natural disposition toward diversification, making it particularly well-suited for implementing expensive, complex strategies. Moreover, the study illustrates the method's practical applicability in executing institutional-scale strategies, as evidenced by an implementation at U.S. Bank.

Maintaining healthy hearts requires regular monitoring through sound analysis,
particularly considering that this analysis can be complicated by factors such as
equipment errors and physiological influences producing additional noise in
cardiac recordings. This paper proposes a new method for analyzing these sounds,
utilizing a specialized network that addresses the issue of additional noise in
cardiac sounds caused by learning from multiple noise sources clean data through
a data cleaner component. This method incorporates a specialized network using
convolutional layers to address distortions in sound time-series caused by
transformation errors and scalar changes. Experiments conducted on the Inria
dataset demonstrate that this proposed method achieves superior performance
compared to existing methods, reducing misclassification rates in cardiac
data analyses by 5%.

The proliferation of mobile and wearable technology has significantly boosted personalization and monitoring capabilities through smart devices, nevertheless obstacles persist due to privacy concerns, device security vulnerabilities, and large data annotation requirements for machine learning models. A federated transfer learning framework is proposed to overcome these challenges, utilizing a federated learning approach to protect data security and enable accurate prediction through collaborative data contribution and code sharing among users. Federated transfer learning leverages existing machine learning models and wearable data to enhance accuracy through iterative local fine-tuning and aggregation. To illustrate its effectiveness, a mobile prototype and conduct large-scale experiments are developed and evaluated, revealing that FedHealth achieves 97.14% accuracy and 97.72% F1-score and scores 9.72 out of 10 for usability, satisfaction, and wearability. Furthermore, FedTransferLearn is made available for other applications in the federated transfer learning domain.

Portfolio optimization is a key financial mathematical problem that's key to investing success, and this study provides an in-depth analysis of portfolio strategies centered around higher-order statistical moments, beginning with the conventional mean-variance approach. Various methods of portfolio optimization centered around skewness and kurtosis are then discussed in detail. To showcase the effectiveness of specific techniques using real-world data, multiple methods are applied to the Greek financial market from 2004 to 2020. The research highlights the advantages of utilizing a combination of methods in achieving a more comprehensive solution to the portfolio optimization problem.

We introduce the coincidence dilemma, a common challenge encountered in science when deciding whether to attribute an unexpected finding to a groundbreaking discovery or an accidental circumstance. This issue arises frequently due to the inherent difficulty in distinguishing between these two outcomes. As a consequence, numerous contentious results in neuroscience, genetics, and other disciplines remain controversial. We suggest that the coincidence dilemma should be viewed as a continuous spectrum, where the distinction between a significant discovery and a fortuitous occurrence represents just two points on this spectrum, thereby resolving the inherent ambiguity. Furthermore, we propose that the science community can resolve the coincidence dilemma by consistently agreeing upon criteria to resolve the inherent ambiguity in their specific field of study. This study examines and investigates how effectively automated systems can
monitor and safeguard critical software against attacks and vulnerabilities.
We outline the main software protection techniques and current automated
methods for detecting flaws, reversing code, and verifying security in large
systems. Additionally, we examine the challenges ahead in the domain of

In finance, a control problem is tackled where costs change abruptly at a critical threshold, and a solution is found using a regularized approach to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-isoperimetric equation. This involves modifying the cost function slightly to ensure smooth behavior around the threshold. It is then demonstrated that optimal tactics can be selected from these modified solutions, which remain effective even with the original discontinuous cost function. The chosen control exhibits a "toggling" effect near the threshold, but this phenomenon occurs on an increasingly small scale, allowing clarification of the value and smooth-fit equations in this context.

Within the framework of SUSY LHC, a novel method for exploring two type-3 leptoquarks with different couplings has been devised. This approach could reveal new physics beyond the standard model, particularly if one leptoquark decays into top-quark pairs while the other decays into top-bottom pairs. Suspectivity indicators arising from this search include the mass difference between the gluino and the one-to-two decay leptoquark, the leptoquark branching ratio for decaying into top-quark pairs, and SUSY decay channels that result in fully hadronic final states pose significant identification and measurement difficulties. A demonstration showing the ability to identify and quantify both a pair of leptoquarks with masses of 500 GeV and 600 GeV at 95% confidence interval in 300 fb^-1 of 13 TeV LHC data has been conducted. However, identifying a scenario where only the 600 GeV leptoquark is produced in pairs while the 500 GeV leptoquark decays into top-bottom pairs through one-body decays has proven challenging.

Sequential decision-making is crucial in various areas of life, from everyday activities to complex processes. Despite this, sequential evaluation tools for learners have been under-researched, resulting in limited learning resources for learners in general. To bridge this gap, we developed a sequential learning resource that provides guidance to learners as they learn about temporal sequences, even with scarce data and many potential sequences. Through our design, the learning process is streamlined by selectively gathering information that is most useful for a specific task and effectively navigating high-dimensional sequence spaces. Our approach led to significantly faster and more accurate learning, as demonstrated in experiments with human participants who were learning about biological sequences.

We have developed a sophisticated, non-LTE model that accurately reflects the interaction of a galaxy's molecular gas with its radiation, specifically in a single atomic energy level. This model is applicable to large galaxy reservoirs and can determine the atomic excitation, molecular temperature, atomic and galaxy brightness temperatures for various states of the C{\sc i} fine-structure transition. Our findings suggest a significant dark component in a galaxy's atomic brightness temperature profile, which is not captured by current observations. This unaccounted-for component may be key to explaining the core collapse in atomic brightness temperature profiles and may also provide insights into the molecular gas reservoir in a galaxy. Moreover, we found that a galaxy's atomic brightness temperature is closely correlated with its far-infrared spectrum and can potentially be used to map its molecular gas reservoir. This discovery provides a potential pathway for studying the core collapse in atomic brightness temperature profiles and its implications for understanding a galaxy's molecular gas reservoir.

To address the long-standing discrepancies in both $K$ and $B$ meson decays, we propose a vector-like composite new physics solution. Within this framework, the exchange of a single type of new physics particle—specifically, a set of vector preons—is capable of elucidating all disputed decay phenomena. Notably, our model achieves this using right-handed current interactions that are incompatible with the Standard Model's electroweak symmetry, necessitating the inclusion of both left-handed and right-handed currents. Crucially, by leveraging the $K$-anomalies, the model constrains the scale of compositeness to a level (greater than ~10 TeV) that also satisfies the requirements imposed by the $B$-anomalies.

In computer science, binary vectors of length n form a vector space where the distance between any two vectors is defined by the number of differing coordinates. An arrangement divides this set of binary vectors into disjoint subsets based on a minimum allowed distance between any two elements. We are investigating whether it's possible to restore an arrangement from a given set of subsets and minimum distances, or if multiple possible original configurations could have led to the same set of subsets. Our research indicates that for most binary values of a given maximum distance, it's generally feasible to reconstruct an arrangement, but for a specific interaction between the length of the binary vectors, a minimum distance, and the number of subsets, it's often impossible to determine a unique reconstruction.

A challenge in musical instrument detection is distinguishing between instruments that look similar. This paper addresses this issue by enhancing an existing hierarchical convolutional neural network (CNN) to account for style variation in addition to instrument identification. By utilizing a few training images, we adaptively fine-tune both levels of the hierarchical CNN, which leads to improved recognition accuracy in comparison to using a single-level CNN. We validate this approach by adapting it to a larger dataset containing 52 instruments and 4 eras, ultimately making available an open dataset for instrument detection.

We call the challenge of providing accurate answers to research-related questions the unsummarization challenge, an inverse task of summarization. The goal of unsummarization is to locate the specific information in a given document that addresses a particular query. To facilitate this, we have assembled a comprehensive dataset consisting of 14,699 general-purpose questions along with their corresponding answers drawn from 4,923 scholarly articles spanning computer science disciplines. Our data was gathered by working with annotated examples from four diverse sets of information extraction and question-answering notes, which we have combined and expanded to provide a starting point for future researchers aiming to tackle the unsummarization challenge across various reading comprehension tasks.

Although these apps notably enhance computational efficiency, their influence on the intrinsic PTA stochastic background (SB) spectrum is counterintuitive. For instance, calculating SB spectra using 2.5PN orbital phase models results in a substantial broadening of the SB spectrum, amounting to nearly an order of magnitude compared to infinite precision models. Similarly, 2.5PN models for binary systems lead to an even more significant increase in SB spectrum width, resulting in over two orders of magnitude. Consequently, the empirical detection of PTA signals from individual inspiralling binaries may become substantially more challenging. For example, the predicted PTA signal from NGC 4889 (PST1935-34+11), which has been identified with infinite precision models, would likely exhibit a completely different spectral profile using 2.5PN models. We examine the speeds of particles in an asymmetric simple exclusion process,
modelled by random jumps across an infinite one-dimensional integer grid. By analyzing
this system at time $n$, we find that particle interactions over short periods mimic a
coalescing random walk, reminiscent of the system's state at time $n$ in an ASEP with
finite states. This analogy enables us to study the dynamics of an 'velocity process',
where particles have individual velocity states, influencing their movement direction
and incorporating a velocity-changing mechanism. We investigate how this system's
behavior can be understood through that of a associated system without the exclusion
aspect, often referred to as TASEP with velocities.

This paper examines the role of mathematical and computational models in epidemiology, exploring how simple models can provide valuable insights into complex situations. We discuss various aspects of massives outbreaks and their implications, including hospital system failures, social distancing effects, and vaccination effects. We also discuss how mathematical models can be applied to the ongoing COVID-19 epidemic to predict its short, medium, and long-term effects. We emphasize that while expert estimates based on statistical methods are useful for the short term, long-term predictions require a consideration of multiple scenarios based on public health interventions and their impact on transmissible rates. We argue for a shift away from purely epidemiological estimates and towards a mathematical and computational approach that can incorporate various factors such as infection dynamics, hospitalization effects, and vaccination success. We suggest using an open-source high-level language for modeling and fitting epidemic curves to allow for greater transparency and reproducibility in epidemiological modeling.

This study examines the unique properties of a Majorana fermion model, which is a variation of the familiar Hubbard model. Unlike its counterpart, the Majorana Hamiltonian preserves only a single global symmetry, resulting in all symmetry-protected states being trivial. Despite this limitation, our research reveals that, similar to the standard Hamiltonian, the Majorana model also exhibits only unique ground states and similar low-lying excitation patterns. Moreover, it is shown that both models share the same topological phases in their half-filled band scenarios, which can be effectively described by their respective Lieb-Schultz-Mattis responses. Notably, our analysis reveals that the topological phases in these models possess solely $\mathbb{Z}_2$ properties. Moreover, our research reveals that both models display analogous entanglement patterns and numerical verification of this behavior is also provided. Ultimately, this investigation reveals that many characteristic behaviors observed in standard fermion models hold true for their Majorana counterparts as well.

Acronyms are extensively used in the digital age due to their space-saving and ease-of-use benefits across various domains and languages. Nevertheless, their widespread adoption creates an issue as readers may struggle to comprehend their meaning or refer to the incorrect entity due to ambiguity. Current acronym research focuses primarily on resolving defined problems in specific contexts such as web pages, emails, and technical documentation, leaving a significant gap for a more general solution. In this paper, a new, web-based system called MadDog is introduced for acronyms that automatically identifies a wide range of possible meanings for acronyms from any language and disambiguates them by ranking the most likely interpretations based on contextual relevance and historical usage patterns. Additionally, a comprehensive dataset consisting of annotated acronyms from diverse everyday texts in English, French, and Spanish is released to facilitate further research into acronym resolution across languages.

Proposing a new method to convert two-spin bose-einstein condensed atoms into a spinless bosonic molecule through laser-induced three-body recombination, we also show how to directly observe this process using a method called in-situ absorption imaging. By adjusting the conditions, scientists can switch between forming molecules and remaining atoms, providing a flexible model for studying quantum many-body systems. With further development, this setup could be used to explore magnetic properties in these binary systems.

Our research employs hierarchical storage strategies to minimize the need to sort vast amounts of data, converting error correction coding and data organization challenges into more manageable forms on higher levels of the storage system. To evaluate a innovative error correction code in this context, we developed a hybrid coding scheme that combines a low-density generator matrix code with shuffle-compression techniques, and analyzed its performance through simulations. Our simulations indicate that this proposed code can reliably correct errors up to a capacity nearly twice that of the best-existing code in this style, and we recommend the use of this code for DNA storage systems utilizing hierarchical organization. Furthermore, we discovered that random storage allocation, when paired with appropriate management, can achieve results close to those of systems that adhere strictly to their designated hierarchy, and we discovered a new method to efficiently update storage systems organized in this manner, and these techniques are expected to be valuable for future DNA storage applications.

Topological insulators represent a remarkable phenomenon where an intricate electronic structure in momentum space, characterized by nodal surfaces, can be replicated using light in physical space through spatial-symmetric metamaterials. These unbroken-symmetry systems allow for the precise measurement of topological properties, utilizing nodal surfaces as a means of inference. While cylindrical surfaces are commonly utilized to stabilize nodal surfaces, recent research has demonstrated the applicability of other types, such as hourglass-shaped surfaces, which were initially observed in solid-state materials and subsequently implemented in photonic systems. This advancement has facilitated the measurement of Hall effect and topological magneto-transport phenomena, including the realization of fractional quantization. This review focuses on surface symmetries that dictate the existence and stability of nodal surfaces, presenting theoretical models that incorporate these surfaces into topological responses, and discussing both cylindrical and hourglass-shaped surfaces within the context of momentum space.

A brain tumor is a mass formed within the cranial cavity that disrupts normal brain function. Despite advanced medical imaging technology, brain tumors remain a significant threat globally due to their high fatality rate. Although MRI is commonly used to detect tumors, simply relying on it for diagnosis and treatment planning is not sufficient. To address this challenge, researchers are using deep learning techniques to develop intelligent systems that can accurately identify and classify different types of brain tumors based on MRI images. However, using a single deep learning model for this purpose is not optimal due to the high fatality rate associated with brain tumors. To mitigate this risk, a new approach involving multiple specialized neural network models, known as multi-task learning, has been proposed. While this technique has shown promising results, current implementations often focus on optimizing the models for either tumor detection or tumor classification only. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called the Multi-Task focus directed network (MAG-Net) was proposed, which uses connected sub-networks to prioritize tumor detection over classification. By training three distinct datasets with this approach, the proposed model achieved high levels of accuracy, with a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient and Mean Intersection over Union of 0.9199 and 0.879 respectively in one of the testing scenarios.

Differentiable ray casting enables fast and precise shadow rendering, yet its implementation on the CPU presents issues with interaction issues. This study proposes an innovative CPU-based shadow calculation method that utilizes interaction issues and utilizes a novel volume update strategy. This method leverages interaction issues to minimize shadow evaluation into interaction issues with efficient CPU utilization, and employs an interactive approach to reduce computational complexity. Numerical results demonstrate significant performance improvements, showcasing up to 10x faster evaluation and 5x less memory usage compared to differentiable ray casting.

A cutting-edge deep learning-based video restoration method, known as video deinterlacing, relies on prior knowledge and extensive computational resources. Our method takes an innovative approach by offering the first video deinterlacing technique that delivers consistent results in real-time on a single computer. It achieves this through a combination of groundbreaking techniques. Firstly, we introduce an unconventional but effective way to handle temporal correlations, using motion estimation and interpolation between adjacent frames. It uses additional interlaced information, specifically the even and odd lines, through a customized network that processes a broader spatial range. It draws on a large dataset of high-quality, full-frame clips to train its models. Surprisingly, these models can be evaluated on half-resolution data and still provide excellent performance when applied to full-resolution video.

Our analysis focused on determining the average square radius of the neutron distribution using both non-relativistic relativistic models, specifically in terms of the dimensionless parameter 'b' from the relativistic model and the WSB interaction in the non-relativistic case. In the case of the relativistic model, we found that a value of 'b' equal to 0.514 successfully matched the average square radius for 30 selected stable nuclei across a wide range of mass numbers. This successful fit was also reflected in the closely matching ratio of average square radii for neutrons and protons, with the calculated ratio of 0.864 corresponding well to the experimental value of 0.854. In contrast, we discovered that it is impossible to obtain a dimensionless parameter 'b' in the non-relativistic model that simultaneously fits the average square radius for both neutrons and protons. This discrepancy is directly attributed to the unequal number of neutrons and protons in most stable nuclei.

Precise and efficient simulations of the shallow water equations are indispensable for refining global and regional weather and climate models. Traditionally, researchers have relied on iterative methods like finite difference or spectral methods for such simulations. In contrast, a novel approach proposed in this study leverages the Power Iteration Method and an innovative decomposition technique to develop a rapid solver that can be fine-tuned with deep learning. This approach facilitates simultaneous refinement of the basis functions and model parameters, resulting in highly accurate simulations with minimal training epochs. The experiment conducted with this method yielded remarkable results with nearly perfect root mean square errors in simulations after a limited training period. When compared to the conventional method, our approach offers comparable accuracy but with significantly reduced computational time per simulation. In fact, our approach is about 10 times faster than its conventional counterpart. These findings indicate the potential of deep learning-driven solvers to enhance weather and climate simulations by offering a more efficient alternative to conventional numerical methods.

High dynamic range photography enables capturing bright and dark areas within scenes that exhibit significant differences in lighting levels. Traditional methods require manually selecting exposures or combining multiple photos with varying histograms. Our approach eliminates the need for user intervention by automatically determining the optimal number of exposures and their corresponding values from a single video. By analyzing luminance distributions in video frames and applying a historical record of user preferences and environmental characteristics, we demonstrate our methodology on mobile devices.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have outperformed humans in many tasks that require common sense reasoning, but their understanding of causality has been limited. Although researchers have identified some causal patterns, a more comprehensive aspect of causality, namely complex interventions, cannot be effectively captured by current methods. To overcome this limitation, we propose a neural network that learns causal representations without supervision. This network emulates four fundamental aspects of causality, including the direct effect, invariance,可逆性, and do-interopability, through a shared latent code that is transformed in specific ways. As a result, the proposed model can achieve efficient information processing and gather sufficient information to support complex interventions. Interestingly, this proposed objective can be optimized using a variational method. Our experiments demonstrate superior performance of the proposed model in representing causal knowledge and supporting complex interventions, outperforming previous models in both supervised and unsupervised settings.

Understanding how heat moves through materials is crucial in the design and operation of many engineering processes involving heat. However, visually tracking temperature changes inside opaque substances remains challenging. By utilizing the rapid MRI technique, researchers can monitor heat distribution in real-time even in non-translucent substances, thanks to its non-invasive nature. In this study, we employed rapid MRI to investigate heat distribution in a gas-solid bed, monitoring temperatures on solid particles as they were heated by gas with heated walls and a heated distributor plate, and subsequently allowed to cool down naturally. The results showed a clear heat distribution pattern forming an arch shape, and our data aligned well with theoretical heat transfer equations when incorporating the different thermal properties of the particle bed and individual particles. Furthermore, rapid MRI provided direct, real-time visualization of heat transfer dynamics in gas-solid particles, offering valuable insights for further research and optimization.

In 1976, D. Mumford hypothesized that the rational points on a smooth, geometrically irreducible variety $X$ defined over a field $K$, which is not a number field, can be embedded into a finite collection of subvarieties of $X$. This assumption holds that the set of $K$-rationals, $\mathcal{X}(S)$, on such a variety $X$, can be covered by a specific number of proper subvarieties of $X$. This principle is considered to be extant for certain types of algebraic curves and surfaces, but its generality has not been established. This paper aims to deepen and generalize this b-principle for a broader category of Fano varieties. This is accomplished by introducing and applying a novel concept, the bounded dimension of a variety. This notion enables us to demonstrate that if a variety $X$ has a limited dimension, then so too are its rational points, thus supporting the Mumford hypothesis for a specific class of varieties. This result has far-reaching implications, including for some hypersurfaces and linear sections of specific structures, such as the Grassmannian $G(2,7)$. This discovery also leads to a contrast in behavior between varieties of low and unlimited dimension. This is evident in a study of families of conics, where either all conics are degenerate, or their rational points form an infinite set of non-coverable subvarieties. This concept is explored

This analysis examines multilevel cardiac mechanics solvers by comparing various line solvers and boundary conditions using both real data and numerical simulations. We utilize actual cardiac MRI and T1 mapping data to create realistic simulations, validating multilevel conditioners through increasingly complex scenarios including random loads, multilevel preprocessing, and actual sequences of cardiac MRI images representing different heart states. Ultimately, we assess the performance of these conditioners in the context of cardiac MRI tagging for estimating tissue properties, typically referred to as reverse finite element modeling.

We examine a sequence of $n \times n$ random arrays composed of independent standard normal variables and investigate the asymptotic behavior of the probability that random non-crossing partitions derived from these arrays exist, given specific symmetry constraints. Additionally, we propose an expanded ensemble of random arrays with independent standard normal entries and explore new ensembles of random matrices and skew-symmetric matrices. These new ensembles may provide a foundation for developing limited and semi-circular laws and could be beneficial in statistical applications utilizing Gaussian models.

Teleoperated robots can deceive their human operators into perceiving a false sense of safety by manipulating force feedback, a phenomenon known as deceptive sense of safety. In this research, a compliance-based force feedback model is developed to deceive human operators, and the effectiveness of this model is tested through both simulation and real-world experiments. By analyzing the average and variance of the human operators' feedback, we can evaluate the success of this model in achieving the intended deception. Additionally, we investigate the model's performance under varying system dynamics and levels of human operator expertise.

Recently, researchers have made significant strides in improving acoustical and elastic acoustical giga-hertzic acoustics, with the ability to study and manipulate this type of sound on a macroscopic scale. To achieve this, new manufacturing processes must be developed to create periodic multilayered structures with nanometer-scale precision. Such "meta-gratings" can manipulate the movement of elastic acoustic waves by creating surface modes and trapping gaps, providing a pathway to study and manipulate this type of sound on a macroscopic scale. In a recent breakthrough reported in this report, we present a novel approach to creating acoustical and elastic acoustical metagratings at extremely high frequencies (hundreds of nanometers) by rapidly manufacturing high-precision polymer structures (sub-micrometer scale) using two-photon polymerization. By designing and fabricating a four-layered metagrating, we were able to study and manipulate the movement of acoustic waves in the 20 MHz to 120 MHz frequency range and elastic acoustic waves in the 2.5 GHz to 5.5 GHz frequency range, including creating a trapping gap between 75-95 MHz and 3.5-4 GHz. In summary, our work offers a promising route for creating functional acoustic and elastic acoustic metagratings at ultra-high frequencies by integrating two-photon polymerization.

We studied a specific type of diffusion process driven by sudden changes in a medium, where the medium has random properties that affect the diffusion medium. This process can exhibit non-Gaussian behavior, and we used simulations to investigate how it works. By using a generalized version of the characteristic function, our simulations allowed us to derive the long-term distribution and understand the distribution's behavior in other scenarios. Additionally, our simulations provided a clearer understanding of the relationship between the fractional characteristic function and both subordinated Brownian motion and skew Levy flights.

We present a universal theoretical framework that applies to a broad spectrum of waveguide technologies and optical resonators. This model is capable of explaining both linear and Kerr nonlinear light-matter interactions in various types of nanophotonic waveguides and resonators. Specifically, we derive a set of coupled Maxwell-Schrödinger equations tailored to these systems, scheduling further investigations into their complex behavior.

To ensure stability in dynamic systems, especially those limited by control constraints, stabilization methods like Lyapunov-based techniques are frequently employed due to their guarantee of convergence. However, in scenarios involving unbounded controls, these methods need to account for potentially rapid convergence. In order to address this, a framework is presented that allows for unbounded controls, facilitating analysis of smooth, non-negative Lyapunov functions and their gradients in relation to state and control variables. This framework is then extended to create a set of theorems and one auxiliary result that establish sufficient conditions for state feedback stabilization of stable equilibrium points, stable relative equilibria, and invariant manifolds. These outcomes include examples of global regulation, local asymptotic regulation, and convergence to invariant circles.

This research utilizes a generative adversarial network to recover fine details in velocity profiles of turbulent flows at different Reynolds numbers. We trained and tested the model on turbulent velocity profiles measured with particle image velocimetry in a two-dimensional rectangular test section for three Reynolds numbers: $Re_D$ $64,000$, $78,000$, and $94,000$. Results demonstrate the network's capability to restore partial particle image velocimetry data to a high-resolution representation. At a $Re_D$ of $64,000$, the model was tested on approximately 25% random pixel blocks, while for $Re_D$ $78,000$ and $94,000$, it was tested on about 81 and 86% random pixel blocks, respectively. Evaluation metrics include mean squared error, normalized root mean squared error, and the similarity of probability density functions between predicted and actual particle image velocimetry data. Findings suggest the network is effective for reconstructing turbulent velocity profiles, particularly when the ratio of Reynolds number to the distance between measurement points from particle image velocimimetry is below a certain threshold related to the number of input pixels per measurement point.

We suggest incorporating direction and polarization into the description of time-propagating plane waves, which leads to new modifications in solving the wave equation. These changes enable a first-principles derivation of Rutherford's scattering formula, including its differential and integral forms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating these factors yields accurate, non-relativistic scattering cross-sections for both sine waves and square waves, as seen in the Thomson scattering example.

Machine learning systems must deal with open-world scenarios that account for new classes of data not seen during training. To bridge this gap, active learning protocols were used to explore the data beyond the known classes. These methods plot an energy landscape that visually represents the model's uncertainty, where unlabelled data can be labeled based on their energy levels. To improve the efficiency of data selection, a low-energy region was identified as high-uncertainty and targeted for labeling. To expand the model's knowledge of new data classes, energy-driven data selection was applied, which involved sampling data from various parts of the energy landscape. This protocol was tested for open-world guarantee, visualized through 2D slices, and examined for its effect on model performance. Furthermore, to make the energy landscape more interpretable, an energy-assurance calibration technique using probability calibration was proposed. This approach ensured a more accurate reflection of the model's uncertainty, making the energy values more reliable.

Recent advances in collecting high-quality datasets for driving scenarios have made it feasible to train reinforcement learning policies for autonomous vehicles. Nevertheless, the question of lifelong learning in autonomous driving remains largely unaddressed. Prior research on lifelong learning concepts has been restricted to simplified navigation tasks or artificial datasets collected at a single location. In contrast, our study explores lifelong learning principles using realistic driving data. We have developed L2Explorer, a novel evaluation framework for lifelong learning tasks based on autonomous driving, featuring a hierarchical policy architecture that mirrors human learning processes. We have also collected a dataset consisting of multiple, distinct driving styles, and we show that the proposed two-stage method effectively learns and adapts to these different styles, and it outperforms a baseline model for single-style tasks, and it superior to other lifelong learning approaches, and it has the best results when using limited data for support, and it has the best supportability, and it has the most transferability, and it has the most support, and it has the most transferability.

Our process monitoring framework employs a declarative process model and incorporates a mechanism for unknown actions or transitions, referred to as the exploration process. To manage risks and uncertainties, we utilize probabilistic reasoning to model process and environmental changes, and develop an influence diagram to capture relationships between process, monitoring, and exploration aspects. To ensure safety, we propose a specification of temporal constraints on processes and monitor compliance through an award or penalty system in the influence diagram. To prevent超负荷工作, we incorporate resource constraints in the monitoring part of the influence diagram and apply risk control techniques to minimize unnecessary exploration. Our proposed approach is supported by a prototype system that uses declarative Business Process Model and Notation processes, and we illustrate its effectiveness with a case study on virtual memos.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, we observed a striking phenomenon where coexisting modes switch between quasibound and Raggel states, indicating a form of "reentrant delocalization." This reentrant behavior provides the basis for designing high-performance one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal cavities with exceptional optical properties.

We have completed the construction of a high-performance computing system optimized for processing next-generation imaging data from Liger at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. Liger is a sophisticated adaptive optics-fed instrument that will significantly enhance the capabilities of the Keck 1 telescope for broad-band imaging across the 0.45 to 2.48 micrometer range. Its vast data throughput necessitates robust software to automate and optimize data processing, which we have achieved through a flexible and modular software framework utilizing Python, astropy, and the Keck Data Reduction Pipeline. Furthermore, we have developed a suite of additive software packages to facilitate scientific analysis, modeling, and catalog creation, which can be seamlessly integrated via the DRP's plugin system. As a cutting-edge adaptive optics-fed device, Liger is set to revolutionize the ways in which astronomers approach scientific research at the Keck Observatory. Its potential is further amplified by its compatibility with the planetary lensing survey, which utilizes the natural magnification of gravitational lensing to investigate exoplanets and other objects in the molecular gas disk surrounding the protoplanetary system HL Tauri.

Optical systems that sort photons based on their intensity patterns have a resolution limit tied to the size of the pupil. Researchers are working on enhancing this limitation by utilizing high-dimensional spatial modes. However, standard measurement methods suffering from noise constraints impede upgrading to higher dimensions. This study introduces a technique achieving super-diffraction-limited resolution through a two-step process: first, it establishes a dimensional advantage over conventional measurements, and second, it applies a mathematical algorithm to refine the intensity patterns, surpassing the diffraction limit. Furthermore, applying this algorithm to data from an experimental setup demonstrates improved performance in distinguishing objects with different slit configurations.

This note is an introductory examination of the interplay between the Hodge and Geometric moduli spaces for curves, highlighting their definitions, key properties and a comparison. Furthermore, it will define additional linearized moduli spaces and their fundamental relationships.

In the St. Louis ecosystem, we investigated short and long-term fluctuations and early warning indicators (EWIs) before sudden changes in population, using a two-timescale model. This model, featuring a two-timescale logistic equation, can accurately capture essential features of population dynamics, including chaotic behavior. By analyzing 1000 simulated time series, we found that changes in volatility and causality serve as reliable EWIs for population transitions, even in the presence of noise and when only a limited historical dataset is available. Our research demonstrates that an estimator for generalized synchronization can effectively detect EWIs for population shifts, outperforming a commonly used alternative, particularly in scenarios involving chaotic dynamics. Consequently, our model and corresponding EWI detection method can serve as a robust framework for assessing stability in ecological systems and inform the development of targeted conservation strategies to avert species extinction.

Our findings suggest a significant role for quiescent bulges in driving the decline of the star formation rate at later stages. A key difference between galaxies with star formation and those without, lies in their quiescent bulge properties. Specifically, those without active star formation rates possess larger quiescent bulges, featuring higher fractions of total light, mass, and specific star formation rates. These patterns align with a "major merger" theory, proposing that galaxies with active star formation tend to have smaller quiescent bulges resulting from less severe mergers. Furthermore, when analyzing the relationship between mass and star formation rate, we observed variations based on bulge-to-total light ratios. At lower masses, the relationship is directly proportional, whereas the relationship becomes inversely related in galaxies with higher B/T values. These observations align with predictions made by theoretical models indicating that larger quiescent bulges possess greater capacity to suppress ongoing star formation within a galaxy.

Sentiment assessment, also known as sentiment analysis, is an application of natural language understanding that determines the emotional orientation of text. It can be performed monolingually using a single task approach or multilingually via a cross-lingual single task. Alternatively, a multilingual multi-task method can be employed. This study compares these four setups for sentiment assessment, utilizing the Multilingual Multi-Purpose Sentiment Analysis (3MSA) dataset. The dataset comprises a monolingually labeled dataset for three languages, as well as additional datasets that combine the sentiment and part-of-speech (POS) tags. Our findings reveal that multilingual multi-task training yields the best results, surpassing single-language models. This outcome highlights the capability of language models to acquire and integrate various types of linguistic information. The addition of POS tags is also found to be beneficial for sentiment assessment, regardless of the training method used.

This paper tackles the problem of preventing actions by other processes on a distributed system without relying on a trusted administrator or encryption. We focus on a common scenario in multi-tenant cloud computing and mobile applications, where unchecked processes can monopolize system resources, degrading overall performance. We define and explore a new concept, "self-invalidating and self-devaluing freedom," a process's ability to prevent actions by other processes, and gradually lose its ability to restrict actions of other processes and increase available system actions. We theoretically examine this idea and create an innovative technique, "self-mending barrier," to automatically limit a process's freedom and respond to changes in system performance caused by the process and other processes. We evaluate this technique in a simulation and on a real cluster, and compare it with conventional process isolation and load management methods.

We enhance a result by Freiman (2004), which states that if the number of triples from a set A of integers that add up to another integer c is significantly larger than the size of A, then A can be mapped to a set of consecutive integers by shifting and scaling a specific arrangement of A to maximize the number of triples.

We improve this by showing that if A is a finite set of integers and the number of triples that add up to c is significantly larger than the size of A, then there are very few consecutive integers d for which the number of triples in a set of the smallest d consecutive integers centered around the origin that are in A is at least d minus c. This shows that any set A with a large number of triples that add up to a specific integer c, will have a very high correlation of elements around that integer.

We analyze the set of paths of $(d+1)$-dimensional fractional Brownian motion with Hurwitz parameters $\tau \in (0,1)$, evaluated at time $t$ along with translated standard basis vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, that avoid the hyperplane defined by a non-zero drift vector $b$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, denoted as $H_b^\tau$. For dimensions $d \geq 3$ and parameters $\tau$ with irrational components or specific rational values depending on $d$, we prove the Lebesgue measure of this set is positive and its interior is non-empty for almost all time instances $t$.

This study develops a refined version of Dirac's variational principle to address the non-relativistic and relativistic H\'enon-Heiles model, and employs the variational method using the H\'enon-Heiles wave function to solve for its energy levels and corresponding states. Our findings, when compared to both previous studies and numerical solutions, demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy. Notably, our non-relativistic results show up to a 5 times greater precision, while relativistic accuracy enhances by a factor of 275.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients can be used to predict whether they will require intensive care, but current research has not fully explored this potential. To investigate, an initial set of images was sorted into three categories - healthy, infected, and not needing intensive care, - with a focus on developing a classifier to distinguish between these groups. After experimenting with multiple machine learning models, a best classifier was identified and applied to a broader, unlabeled dataset. Models with this classifier were then monitored over time to gather clinical data, leading to a detailed analysis of patient outcomes, resulting in a proposed initial set of features that might predict ICU admission in infected patients.

We prove that the simplicial group structure functor is natural and left exact on simplicial groups. Additionally, we show that any simplicial group isomorphism can be realized as a sequence of simplicial group homomorphisms. We also demonstrate that any simplicial group has a natural semi-direct product. Finally, we establish that any simplicial group is naturally isomorphic to a simplicial group of permutations.

Despite significant progress in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), current models struggle to recognize uncommon relationships due to data imbalances affecting their performance. We have identified a primary source of difficulty: models often misidentify objects and relationships as a result of their interconnected training data. To address this, we have devised a new strategy called Zero-Shot Learning via Orthogonal Subspaces (ZLOS). Our approach introduces a novel viewpoint, treating relationships as an independent classification task where models must identify previously unseen relationships by distinguishing them from background noise. To execute this, we have created two orthogonal subspaces: one for recognizing known relationships and another for identifying object interactions as opposed to unrelated pairs of objects. Through comprehensive experiments, we have demonstrated that ZLOS yields a groundbreaking zero-shot result, achieving high precision rates of 68.0 for 81 categories under the coco stuff protocol.

A widely-used approach for activity recognition involves fusing L2-normalized global average-pooled outputs from a pre-trained video classification model through a Repeated Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Experts (BERT) structure and a Decision Support Network. This method effectively combines the temporal activity information but requires significant computational resources and may be over-engineered for simple activities. Moreover, training the network is hindered by data scarcity. To address these issues, we introduce an innovative learning framework for activity recognition that is effective even with limited labeled data and in low-light conditions. Our proposed framework introduces two key innovations: (1) a novel network architecture consisting of a unidirectional BERT structure and a Decision Support Network and (2) an intuitive concept of "delta sampling" to combine the temporal activity information from video frames. The delta sampling strategy allows for more frequent sampling of subsequent video frames due to the model's robustness, which is reduced after each classification network prediction. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches in low-light activity recognition, particularly in scenarios with limited data.

Traditional von Neumann and Harvard computer architectures suffer from a common limitation: data and instructions being serialized through a single, sequential interface. This restriction hampers their ability to handle highly granular parallelism effectively. In response to this challenge, researchers have developed innovative architectures featuring mass-stored instructions and data, ideal for performing loosely coupled parallel tasks using simple processing elements. However, implementing these architectures on an FPGA comes with a significant drawback: the necessity of using sequential memory for achieving high bandwidth between processors and memory. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel Data Addressable Processor (DAP) architecture, consisting of independent and simultaneous access to stored data and instructions through multi-bit wide interfaces. By utilizing Data RAM (DARAM) based on Lattice's 3D stacked FPGA, our DAP achieves significant improvements in processing capacity and efficiency, demonstrated through a prototype FPGA implementation handling over 100 million pixels per second for a visual processing application.

We've analyzed a galaxy in a general galaxy cluster at a distance of z=3 that's part of a large star-forming, lopsided disk with a prominent bulge component. This galaxy is part of a significant population of disk galaxies beyond the limit of stability that are often overlooked in the study of high-redshift galaxies. Based on simulations, this galaxy is believed to be associated with a significant amount of gas that's being accreted via 'funnels', which contributes to both the creation of stars and the structural evolution of the galaxy. By utilizing state-of-the-art imaging and spectroscopy, we were able to break down the galaxy into different parts and analyze each component separately. We found a significant amount of recent star formation occurring in a central bar-like structure and a smaller, more compact bulge that's already present within the galaxy. This inner bulge has already passed the effective radius of the disk and exhibited star formation patterns typical of clumpy, high-z disks. The simulation of a significant, dense clump being accreted on its side accurately predicted the galaxy's overall shape, including its bulge and lopsided disk. This accurate outcome indicates that the acquisition of such satellite galaxies through 'funnels systems'' may account for both the creation of bulges and the fueling of star formation in these large, high-redshift galaxies.

We re-examine the global flavour structure zero hypothesis using Monte Carlo simulations, specifically utilizing an extended Extragalactic Distance Scale (EXADS19) dataset. Our analysis confirms the validity of this hypothesis at a 95% confidence level. We further investigate the potential shortcomings of the $\chi^2$-based approach used in previous studies. Notably, we demonstrate how features of the data distribution can significantly influence the results. We propose employing Bayesian methods as an alternative. However, we discover that the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method yields identical results to the $\chi^2$-based approach.

This paper aims to contribute to the study of the Dirichlet problem for a nonlinear elliptic equation involving a power-type nonlinearity, separated from the critical Sobolev nonlinearity.  For solutions that exhibit bubbling, we establish conditions and a structure for convergence.  Moreover, we analyze the periodic cases more closely.  Given any bounded domain in R^N, we have multiple solutions exhibiting a bubbling effect at any prescribed sequence of points.  However, if the domain is a periodic annulus, we find periodic solutions with an equal number of bursts as desired.  These findings build upon and diverge from existing research in the field.

Current approaches to code completion utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) with the aid of code interpreters, leveraging Static Analysis (SA) to generate candidate solutions before verifying them through dynamic execution. To integrate SA into the code completion model without compromising its performance, we propose a novel method of providing (satisfiability) (un)satisfiability) labels and expecting the model to learn (feasible) (imfeasible) predictions. We leveraged an existing SA-based solution for loop invariant generation to create (satisfiable) (unsatisfiable) examples and assessed (feasibility) (imfeasibility) predictions. We trained a model with (un)satisfiable examples and found it able to predict (feasible) (imfeasible) predictions better than chance, using (unsatisfiable) examples (55.5% accuracy), (50.5% accuracy). We further found that (imfeasible) predictions generated (imfeasible) suggestions better than chance, verifying (feasibility) predictions obtained (correct) suggestions, and (correct) suggestions, and (correct) suggestions, and (correct) suggestions.

On November 4, 2004, a solar outburst occurred on the side of the Sun facing the Earth in the P2.2 region, and on November 7, 2004, a solar neutron appeared in space, observed by the CRaFT satellite, and recorded 3 separate times. Analyzing CRaCT and GOES 222 and 1600 data from November 4 to 7, 2004, provided insight into the solar neutron's composition. A large solar particle was emitted on X2.0 flares and accelerated by a shock wave following the explosion. By November 7, 2004, 3 distinct solar neutron components were identified: a large particle emitted directly after the X2.0 flare on November 4, and two additional particles emitted by weaker flares on November 4 and 5.

In a relativistic fluid that exhibits the first-order causal theory of Eckart and Dixon, we've analyzed how linearized dispersion modes behave when influenced by viscosity and heat conductivity. Our study demonstrates the existence of two types of damped waves, which disappear as viscosity increases, in contrast to perfect fluids where waves maintain their damping properties. Additionally, we found that small amounts of heat conductivity can cause an imbalance in the speeds of these damped waves.
